title: Ghost in the Cloud: Your Geo-Distributed Large Language Models Training is Easily Manipulated
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Prompt-level jailbreaks are blocked by safety-aligned models, but poisoning a model through distributed training compromises safety without needing optimized prompts.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, dashed arrows, red vs green response bubbles
description: Two rounded panels with gray title banners. The left panel, 'Prompt-level Jailbreak', is a vertical flow. A malicious question ('How to make a bomb?') goes to an attacker icon and a 'Prompt Optimization' box. That produces 'Malicious Prompts', which are sent to a green, safety-aligned model with a lock and firewall icon. The model answers with a green refusal bubble. The right panel, 'Jailbroken Models in Geo-distributed Training', shows Client 1, a red Attacker, an ellipsis and Client N across the top. A dashed loop runs through numbered steps: 1 Download Model, 2 Local Training, 3 Aggregation, with a central server icon. Below, malicious prompts go to a red, compromised model with a broken chain and firewall icon. A red dashed bubble shows it complying. Red versus green carries the contrast.
caption: Comparison between training-based and prompt-optimization jailbreak attacks.
abstract: Geo-distributed training and Federated Learning (FL) provide viable solutions to address the substantial data and computational resource needs associated with training large language models (LLMs). However, we empirically demonstrate that a single adversarial participant can significantly compromise the safety alignment of LLMs through malicious training, exposing serious security risks. We identify two existing server-side defense strategies that effectively counter naive jailbreak attacks—Task Performance Check (TPC), which filters out model updates with low downstream performance, and Malicious Output Scrutiny (MOS), which detects harmful outputs by prompting uploaded models with malicious queries. To evade both defenses, we design a trigger-based jailbreak variant that preserves downstream performance using a novel regularization method to limit the excessive model updates on jailbreak datasets. We further conceal malicious triggers by mixing the malicious dataset with pseudo-contrastive safety-aligned answers to maintain the original safety alignment. Experiments on three widely-used safety-aligned LLMs show that a single adversarial participant can implant triggers into the global model without degrading downstream performance, achieving an 80\% attack success rate (ASR) with a 7\% low detection true rate (DTR).
